{{Short description|UK statistical survey}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2023}}
The '''British Social Attitudes Survey''' ('''BSA''') is an annual [[statistical survey]] conducted in the UK by the [[National Centre for Social Research]] since 1983.<ref name=UKDA>{{cite web|url=http://discover.ukdataservice.ac.uk/series/?sn=200006|title=British Social Attitudes Survey catalogue page]|publisher=UK Data Service|accessdate=8 November 2013}}</ref> The BSA involves in-depth interviews with over 3,000 respondents, selected using [[Survey sampling|random probability sampling]],<ref name="NatCen">{{cite web|url=http://www.natcen.ac.uk/series/british-social-attitudes|title=British Social Attitudes|date=September 2011|publisher=National Centre for Social Research|accessdate=19 September 2011}}</ref> focused on topics including [[newspaper]] readership, [[political parties]] and trust, [[public expenditure]], [[welfare benefits]], [[health care]], [[childcare]], [[poverty]], the [[labour market]] and the [[wiktionary:Workplace|workplace]], [[education]], [[charity (practice)|charitable giving]], the [[countryside]], [[transport]] and the [[Environmental policy|environment]], the [[European Union]], [[economy|economic prospects]], [[Race (classification of humans)|race]], [[religion]], [[civil liberties]], [[immigration]], [[Sentence (law)|sentencing]] and [[prison]]s, [[fear of crime]] and the portrayal of sex and [[violence]] in the [[Mass media|media]].<ref>[http://www.bsa-30.natcen.ac.uk/ 30th British Social Attitudes report], NatCen Social Research, retrieved 8 November 2013</ref>
The survey is funded by [[government department]]s, [[QUANGO|quasi-governmental bodies]], charities and think tanks. The BSA was not conducted in 1988 and 1992, when funding was devoted instead to studies of voting behaviour and political attitudes in the British Election Study.<ref name=UKDA/>

== Findings ==

=== Abortion ===
[[File:British Social Attitudes Survey (2).png|thumb|380x380px|Attitudes towards abortion, 1983–2016]]
{{See also|Abortion in the United Kingdom}}
The proportion of people who believe abortion should be allowed if a woman does not want a child has increased gradually during the period from 1983 to 2016, from 40% in 1983 to 72% in 2016. Similarly an increasing number of people believe abortion should be allowed if a couple cannot afford a child, which reached a high of 68% in 2016. Over 90% of people have consistently believed that abortion is acceptable if the pregnancy is a result of rape.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=British Social Attitudes Information System |url=http://www.britsocat.com/Home |access-date=27 June 2022 |publisher=National Centre for Social Research}}</ref>

=== Capital punishment ===
[[File:British Social Attitudes Survey - Capital Punishment.png|thumb|376x376px|"For some crimes, the death penalty is the most appropriate sentence"]]
{{See also|Capital punishment in the United Kingdom}}
Support for the death penalty has gradually decreased from 75% in 1986 to 43% in 2019. From 2014 onwards, less than half of people supported the use of capital punishment.<ref name=":1" />

=== LGBT rights ===
{{See also|LGBT rights in the United Kingdom}}
==== Same-sex relationships ====
[[File:British Social Attitudes Survey - Same-sex relationships.png|thumb|373x373px|Attitudes towards same-sex relationships, 1986–2012]]
17% of people believed same-sex relationships were 'not wrong at all' in 1983 and the proportion of people holding this view reached a low of 11% in 1987 during the height of the [[AIDS pandemic]]. An increasing number of people were comfortable with same-sex relationships during the period 1989-2017 and as of 2018 66% of people do not consider same-sex relationships to be 'wrong at all'.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=BSA 36 – Relationships and gender identity |url=https://www.bsa.natcen.ac.uk/media/39358/5_bsa36_relationships_and_gender_identity.pdf |publisher=National Centre for Social Research}}</ref>

==== Transgender rights ====
{{See also|Transgender rights in the United Kingdom}}
Attitudes towards transgender people were first examined in the 2016 report, which found that 49% of people view prejudice against transgender people as "always wrong", compared with 6% who believe it is "rarely or never wrong". 34% of people believed prejudice against transgender people is only "mostly" or "sometimes" wrong.<ref name=":0" />

=== Social security ===
[[File:BSA - Social Security.png|thumb|372x372px|"Benefits for unemployed people are too low and cause hardship"]]
From 1983 until the late 1990s, most people thought that benefits for the unemployed were too low and caused hardship. Following the election of the [[New Labour|Labour government]] in [[1997 United Kingdom general election|1997]], there was a sharp decline in this view and the majority of people now believed that unemployment benefit was too high until 2016, when an increasing number of people began to consider unemployment benefits as too low and the proportion of people holding this view reached a twenty five year high of 51% in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=British Social Attitudes 38 – New values, new divides? |url=https://www.bsa.natcen.ac.uk/media/39433/bsa38_new-values-new-divides.pdf |access-date=27 June 2022 |publisher=National Centre for Social Research}}</ref>
